result: Kang et al. (2011) demonstrated that intrahepatic injection of oncogenic NrasG12V induces cellular senescence in hepatocytes (marked by p16 and p21 expression), and that these senescent cells are progressively cleared over 60 days through an adaptive immune response. Immunocompromised SCID/beige mice showed significantly attenuated clearance, demonstrating the necessity of functional adaptive immunity for senescence surveillance.
evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C13-C21 collectively describe findings from the original Kang et al. 2011 study that are well-documented with specific figure references (Figures 2I, 3B, 3C, 3E). The experimental approach using hydrodynamic injection, time-course analysis, and immunocompromised mouse models provides converging evidence for oncogene-induced senescence and immune-mediated clearance.

result: Kang et al. (2011) demonstrated the specific requirement for CD4+ T cells in senescence surveillance. CD4−/− mice showed significantly impaired clearance of Nras-positive hepatocytes at 12 days post-injection compared to wild-type mice, while neither CD4−/− nor wild-type mice cleared cells expressing the non-signaling mutant NrasG12V/D38A.
evaluation: Claims C4, C22-C25 describe findings from Figure 4A of Kang et al. 2011 demonstrating CD4+ T cell specificity. The use of CD4−/− mice and the non-signaling mutant control (NrasG12V/D38A) provides strong evidence for the specific role of CD4+ T cells in immune surveillance of senescent hepatocytes.

result: Cellular senescence is a permanent proliferative arrest that serves as a tumor suppression mechanism. Oncogene activation can induce senescence, which is associated with pre-malignant states, and senescent cells have been observed in various cancers.
evaluation: Claims C5-C9 present well-established background knowledge about cellular senescence supported by appropriate citations (Narita and Lowe 2005; Quintanilla et al. 1986; Braig et al. 2005; Collado et al. 2005; Bennecke et al. 2010). These are accepted concepts in the field.

result: Immune surveillance, defined as the immune system's ability to identify and eliminate pre-cancerous cells, is an ongoing area of debate in cancer biology. This concept has generated interest in developing pro-senescent cancer therapies.
evaluation: Claims C10-C12 accurately describe the state of the field regarding immune surveillance with appropriate citation (Swann and Smyth 2007). These claims provide context for the significance of the work being replicated.

result: Multiple studies have reported conflicting results regarding Ras-induced senescence and immune clearance. While some studies (Kennedy et al. 2011, Xue et al. 2007, Rakhra et al. 2010, Acosta et al. 2013) support senescence induction and immune clearance, others (Ho et al. 2012) failed to detect senescence markers. Context-dependent factors such as co-expression of other oncogenes or different oncogenic drivers can prevent senescence surveillance.
evaluation: Claims C26-C34 accurately summarize the conflicting literature on oncogene-induced senescence and immune surveillance with appropriate citations. This provides important context showing that the phenomenon being studied is not universally observed and depends on experimental conditions.

result: The replication study (Protocol 1) will use a minimum of 5 mice per treatment group (starting with 7 to account for ~20% injection failure rate) to achieve 89.8-99.9% statistical power. Strict exclusion criteria are defined for unsuccessful hydrodynamic injections (>10 seconds or resistance encountered).
evaluation: Claims C35-C40 describe the experimental design and power calculations for the replication study. The sample size justification is based on power calculations from the original data, and the 20% failure rate is attributed to information from the original authors. The exclusion criteria are clearly defined.

result: The replication study differs from the original in several ways: it evaluates only days 6 and 30 (not 12, 60, or 7 months); compares only wild-type and SCID/beige mice (not SCID alone); and stains for Nras, p16, and p21 (but not pERK).
evaluation: Claims C41-C46 clearly document known differences between the replication and original study. These are transparently stated limitations that reduce the scope of the replication while maintaining focus on the key findings.

result: The replication study (Protocol 2) will use a minimum of 5 mice per treatment group (starting with 7) to achieve 94.6% power, evaluating only CD4−/− and wild-type mice at 12 days post-injection. The original study also included antibody-depleted mice, CD8−/− mice, Cd1d−/− mice, and a 7-month timepoint.
evaluation: Claims C47-C50 describe the experimental design for Protocol 2 and document differences from the original study. The power calculation is based on original data, and the scope reduction is clearly stated.

result: Original data from Kang et al. (2011) Figures 3B, 3C, and 3E show that wild-type mice clear Nras-, p21-, and p16-positive hepatocytes from ~15% at day 6 to near 0% by day 30, while SCID/beige mice maintain 10-13% positive cells at day 30, demonstrating impaired clearance.
evaluation: Claims C51-C62 present quantitative data extracted from the original study with means, standard deviations, and sample sizes. These data form the basis for power calculations and show clear differences between wild-type and immunocompromised mice in clearance of senescent markers over time.

result: Original data from Kang et al. (2011) Figure 4A show that wild-type mice injected with NrasG12V have 6.1% Nras-positive hepatocytes at day 12, while CD4−/− mice have 18.6%. Both wild-type and CD4−/− mice injected with the non-signaling mutant NrasG12V/D38A maintain ~16-18% positive cells, indicating no clearance.
evaluation: Claims C63-C66 present quantitative data from the original study demonstrating the CD4+ T cell requirement for clearance. The data show that CD4−/− mice fail to clear oncogenic Nras-expressing cells, and that the non-signaling mutant is not cleared in either genotype, supporting the specificity of the immune response.

result: The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology is replicating 50 cancer biology papers published between 2010 and 2012.
evaluation: Claim C1 describes the scope of the Reproducibility Project as stated in the abstract. This is a straightforward description of the project's goals.

result: NrasG12V/D38A is an effector loop mutant incapable of signaling to downstream pathways, serving as a negative control.
evaluation: Claim C17 describes the properties of the control mutant used in the original study. This is an important experimental control that distinguishes signaling-dependent from signaling-independent effects.
